She didn’t | know what that meant, but it didn’t sound good. She also didn’t know what had caused her restoration from backup memories. It must have been a traumatic event—the © automatic process would only be initiated by a shock to the | system—something that damaged the ship’s brain, something that destroyed her own mind. There would be residual damage.

here that she received a shock. She knew that reinitiating a personality from backup memories caused minor problems with memory—that was one of the many things Celtiberian taught her—but she hadn’t expected damage to this extent. It was inexplicable. All the information she'd been given suggested that one could only expect slight memory loss, possibly a series of ticks. Nothing that couldn’t be corrected by the psych rehab programs. But the damage she was seeing would require intensive chemical modifiers, It may even require physical intervention.

In the middle of her own internal explorations, the ship relayed an alarm. It indicated minute but rising levels of a pathogen spreading out from near the damaged portion of the ship. Hoping her own glitches could wait, Meroit dispatched antigens to the site.

The ship’s immune system was supposed to be selfregulating. It had a huge memory bank dedicated to storing data from previous infections. Unfortunately though, much memory had to be cannibalized for backup after the alien missiles detonated. The damage directly caused by radiation

was serious, but it was all the attendant problems which really threatened the mission. Clotting had caused several small strokes in the ship’s brain—killing pilots, and wiping out memory resources, it had been catastrophic, nearly fatal to the ship. Meroit was doing many things manually these days, working with incomplete information and trying to solve problems that specialized cortices of the brain would normally cope with. Most pilots wouldn’t be flexible enough. For that, she had Celtiberian to thank. Most ships would have died. She imagined hundreds of the ships sent out to explore must be floating aimlessly through space, dead from relatively minor problems, Meroit felt ashamed that the human race could be so wasteful—and shame was one of the emotions that had become foreign to humanity long ago. Quickly enough, the levels of pathogen dropped, and she resumed her own self-examination, Meroit was the last of this ship's pilots. Most of them had piloted along with

' three others. They could keep each other free of sachins and act as backups in case one or another died from external damage to the ship’s brain or became corrupted through repeated reinitiation from backup selves. Now, having lost the three pilots who saw her into the world— and a fourth, Celtiberian—Meroit was alone with her troubles,

The ship had passed through two spiral arms and a large portion of the galaxy’s core over the last several thousand years. It had hosted some thirteen generations of pilots and had visited hundreds of thousands of planets, collecting samples at each. And it would have continued for another thousand years but for the loss if its personality seed—the subsystem that made new pilots—to the two alien projectiles. It was Meroit’s responsibility, with the communication systems down, to see the ship home and to deliver the amazing news that Earth had been found. She’d be delivering more if it weren’t for the damaged memory. She had to be certain she’d make it intact without letting little glitches foul her course or her progress.

The alarm went off again, and Meroit knew there must be an entrenched infection. She wondered where it had come from. Fighting the infection would be hastened by her personal investigation and treatment, one of Celtiberian’s tricks. She wished she could access the memories lost when she had been restored, Though the pathogens were still at low levels, she decided to flush the system again in hopes that she could retard the progress of the infection enough to get a clear view when she entered the bloodstream.

Celtiberian had learned a technique to fool the ship into secreting, rather than scabs or leukocytes, a sort of humaniform vessel for carriage of a pilot into the blood. He was always tinkering with things. He had an insatiable lust for trying new things. It never made sense to her, but he seemed to think it should. Celtiberian had taken her into the bloodstream once for no reason at all. He’d shown her how to secrete a proxy body that could explore the inner workings of the ship’s body. She didn’t understand what she might gain by exploring the ship outside of the brain where she lived, Celtiberian was extremely odd. She worried for him, but she supposed that such anomalous personality traits were the inevitable result of spending so much time isolated with the ship’s—humanity’s—memory. The things he must have seen.

She created a proxy body by directing the ship to secrete a mass of muscle and sinew. The secreting organ was conveniently near the damaged area; apparently, the damage had allowed the infection to take hold.

She did a quick calculation to determine how long the ship would last at the current rate of pathogen production. Making antibodies was costly, and an already-injured ship didn’t have the resources to keep up the fight. The only way to survive would be for Meroit to help the ship fight. Even then, it was a long way home, She was thankful for Celtiberian’s idiosyncrasies,

A fifth pilot was superfluous and human history had shown well what happened with idle hands. Eventually, it was decided that Celtiberian would survey the memory damage. He was to check each synapse and cell. Though it was an unusually simple job for an intelligent pilot to do—simple automatic subminds usually handled such menial tasks—it was very time-consuming. The memory was enormous, Tracking down the origin of humanity meant collecting and analyzing samples of life forms and artifacts, comparing records of geomorphology, history... Virtually all of collective human knowledge. Celtiberian had to make sure all of that information was accessible and he went about his job with exceptional vigor. She found it there. The node itself was infected. Antigens continued attaching themselves to Meroit. She hurried her ¢xamination, noting unusual lacerations that didn’t Seem a likely result of an infection.

She needed to be quick since the body she inhabited was very delicate—a mere hint of human form, little more than a bundle of nerves sketching the trace of a tiny-brained body. She could be damaged easily. If she remained in the bloodstream for too long, the antigens could degrade her spinal cord and the proxy body would die. Then, she’d have

a re a il hte be te the memories of Celtiberian. She feared that the ship might also die. Or, in making it home, she would suffer so much brain

that she wouldn’t remember any of the experiences they'd shared. She wondered what had caused her to go through the reinitiation before. Something to do with the infection?

The infection was deeply entrenched, cating away portions of the secretion organ. This was a serious problem, and probably the reason she was being sieged by antigens—her own proxy body had been secreted by the infected organ! Such a situation was intolerable, and she struggled to clean the invagination that housed the pathogens. Slowly at first, Meroit pulled loose cheeselike globules of bacteria, but the infection was deeper than she could reach, She dug with her clawlike spicules.

Meroit felt a trembling in her proxy muscles. She would

have to clean the site thoroughly. Otherwise, she wouldn’t be » able to secrete any more proxy bodies to examine future infections or injuries or other problems that could threaten the life of the ship and destroy the information contained therein.

The antibodies attacked the infection as well as the proxy, 3 not differentiating the one from the other as she tried to help | them fight.

Soon, she could not work efficiently, and she began lashing out at the infection with sinewy limbs and sharp spicules. She

i and in her panic, she inflicted minor lacerations on the wall of the organ.

Soon, she started to break little pieces from the vessel walls, started breaking into little pieces herself. Then, she stopped. She

was doing damage to the ship. And the damage was identical to the lacerations she'd noticed earlier, Meroit had trouble connecting thoughts in this temporary body as its nervous system deteriorated under the siege by the ship’s immune defenses, but a thought was there, What had caused the older lacerations?

She darted for the nervous interface on the secretion organ. She had to get back into ship's brain. She couldn’t let these memories be lost when she was reinitiated. She couldn't let herself go through memory sleep again. She'd done this before, she thought. She'd been here and fought this fight. How many times? The memory damage was extensive. She must be stuck ina cycle of rebirth, fighting, rebirth. How long had this infection been here? How many times had she fought it?

For the first time, she considered her own survival apart from the survival of the ship, the completion of the mission. Her proxy body was coming apart, and she flailed, trying to connect to the interface. If she didn’t, she would repeat this over and over, degrading further each time. Then, she would be dead and so would the memories of Manchu, Jurchen, Ol Cemet...and Celtiberian. She felt she had to protect those memories, though she did not know why.

The nerves were badly damaged, but she could still access the ship’s brain. She calculated that the ship would succumb to infection long before it reached the home systems. If she stayed out here to fight, the ship might make it. But she would not. It was selfish even to consider her own survival when the mission was at stake, and so close to completion. She was charged with bringing the news of Earth back to humanity. She was not charged with no need for the survival of her affinity...her love—for Celtiberian. She had to communicate the location of Earth so that humanity could find what it had lost.

She accessed the ship’s memory, The vast landscape of human history which Celtiberian had found so fascinating had been gone since the stroke, the worst in a series that continued to erase little patches of ship’s memory even now, since he and the other pilots had been killed, since Meroit had been left alone. Now, what little

memory was left was being used to store the information that would allow humanity to find its way back to their original home. She erased that information. She erased the location of Earth, though it would be thousands of years before humanity sent another ship back to the area that this one had already explored, She erased it, and transferred her own memories to the pittance of ship’s memory left. Humanity would condemn her for the selfish decision, and she was ashamed of herself. She felt weak, and not because of the pathogens— though they were attacking her proxy body with vigor.

She had been infected by Celtiberian’s damned idiosyncrasies, his damned curiosity, his damned self-love, and she'd sacrificed the mission for the survival of her own memories. She was angry—anery, like no human had been for thousands of generations—angry at herself and angry at Celtiberian for giving her the ability to feel anger.

She unleashed the anger on the infection, digging at it, attacking it even as the antibodies attacked her, She ripped at the infection, ignoring her own disintegrating proxy body, ignoring the weakening of her arms, ignoring the little pieces of wrenched tissue as the antibodies digested her. Soon, she was

flailing at nothing but the flowing blood. Soon, she could not hold onto the wall, soon her limbs began to fall apart, and she broke up into fragments, carried off by the blood to be reabsorbed by the ship’s liver. She lost consciousness and

Memory sleep was a discomfort Meroit had never before experienced; it was like having your brains passed through the intestinal tract of a large herbivore. She immediately began scanning ship’s systems, saving her own memories for last.
